descricao: Hair type, color and length; face shape and features; height, build, and skin — all in opposite pairs, plus the modifiers that make descriptions sound natural.

secoes.conteudo:
Here is a situation you probably know. Your friend is waiting for you at a busy coffee shop, and they call: 'I can't find you! Where are you?' You say 'I'm here!' That does not help. 'I'm the person... with a face...' Still nothing. What you need is the right vocabulary — words to describe what you look like, fast and clearly.

Describing appearance is one of the most practical skills in any language. We use it to find people in a crowd, to describe someone we just met, to call someone to mind from years ago. In English, this vocabulary comes up constantly — in conversation, in books, in films, everywhere.

In this material, you will learn the key words in pairs: each description alongside its natural opposite, always together. We will move through hair, face, height, body, and skin. And then you will see how small words like **quite** and **fairly** turn simple descriptions into natural, fluent English.

secoes.titulo: Hair Type: Straight / Curly — with Wavy in Between
secoes.conteudo:
The shape of someone's hair is usually the first thing you notice. Three words cover the full range: **straight**, **wavy**, and **curly**. Think of them as three points on a spectrum.

At one end: **straight** hair. **Straight** hair falls flat and smooth, with no curves at all. It lies close to the head and moves as a single, clean shape. At the other end: **curly** hair. **Curly** hair forms tight, round spirals — the kind that spring back when you pull them gently. In the middle: **wavy** hair. **Wavy** hair has gentle, flowing curves — like the letter S drawn loosely. Not flat enough to be **straight**, not tight enough to be **curly**. **Wavy** is the middle ground, and many people sit right there.

The **straight** / **curly** pair is particularly easy to remember because the contrast is so visual. Once you have seen both words in action, neither one is forgettable. And **wavy** becomes easy too — you can almost feel the gentle movement in the word itself.

secoes.titulo: Color and Length: Fair / Dark, Long / Short
secoes.conteudo:
Once you know the shape of someone's hair, the next things to describe are its color and length. Together, these details give you a very complete picture in just a few words.

For color, the main pair is **fair** and **dark**. **Fair** hair is light in color — pale yellow, golden, or light honey tones. You might also hear **blonde**, which describes the same range; both words are equally natural. At the other end: **dark** hair. **Dark** covers a wide range of deeper shades — brown, dark brown, and black. It is the standard, neutral, and appropriate word for darker hair in any context.

Then there is **grey** hair — or **silver**, if you want a more elegant tone. Both describe the color that comes with age. 'She had beautiful **silver** hair' sounds very different from 'she had **grey** hair,' even though the color is the same. The choice between them says something about the speaker's warmth.

One important note: the word **fair** does double duty in English. **Fair hair** means light-colored hair. **Fair skin** means light-colored skin. You will see it in both contexts constantly — it always signals lightness, whether for hair or skin.

For length, the pair is direct: **long** and **short**. **Long** hair falls well past the neck; **short** hair is cut close to the head. In between: **medium-length** or simply **medium**. One specific style worth knowing: a **ponytail** — hair gathered and tied at the back of the head with a band. The moment someone says 'she had her hair in a ponytail,' you know exactly what she looked like.

secoes.titulo: Face and Features: Round / Angular, Clear / Freckled
secoes.conteudo:
Describing someone's face is about more than hair and skin. The shape of the face, the eyes, and small individual details make a description precise and memorable.

For face shape, the most useful pair is **round** and **angular**. A **round** face has soft, curved lines — full cheeks and a gentle jaw. An **angular** face has sharper, more defined edges — the jaw is prominent and the lines are clear. Most faces fall somewhere between these two, but both words give you a starting point.

Eyes are described by color and sometimes shape. The most common colors: **blue**, **green**, **brown**, and **dark** — a neutral and appropriate word for eyes in deeper shades. For shape: **almond-shaped** eyes have elegant, slightly pointed ends. **Wide eyes** are open and expressive. Eyes can be **small** or **large** — simple adjectives that work perfectly well in any description.

Beyond shape and color, two details come up often. **Freckles** are small, light brown spots on the skin — very common on people with **fair** skin, especially on the nose and cheeks. **Wrinkles** are the lines that appear on the face with age — around the eyes, the mouth, the forehead. You might also hear 'laughter lines' — a kinder, warmer way to describe the wrinkles that form from years of smiling.

secoes.titulo: Height and Build: Tall / Short, Slim / Overweight
secoes.conteudo:
Now let's move from the face to the whole picture: how tall someone is and the overall shape of their body.

For height, the pair is direct: **tall** and **short**. **Tall** is above average height; **short** is below. Both words are completely neutral. One thing worth noticing: **short** appears in two different contexts. **Short** hair means not long. **Short** height means below average. Context always makes the meaning clear — but it is good to be aware of this from the start.

For build — the overall shape of the body — the main pair is **slim** and **overweight**. **Slim** describes someone who is pleasantly thin and looks healthy. It is almost always a positive word; when you call someone **slim**, it sounds like a compliment. At the other end: **overweight** is the polite, neutral, and appropriate term for someone who is heavier than average. It is simply a description, without judgment.

Here is a distinction worth making: there is a second word that means something similar to **slim** — **thin**. Both mean 'not heavy,' but they feel different. **Slim** is always positive. **Thin** is more neutral, and sometimes it implies concern — as if the person looks fragile or has lost weight. If you want to pay a compliment, use **slim**. If you are making a purely factual observation about someone who looks very light, **thin** is more precise. Native speakers make this choice automatically.

Beyond the slim / overweight pair: **muscular** describes someone with strong, developed muscles built from regular exercise. It sits on a different axis from **slim** and **overweight** — a **muscular** person can also be **slim**. It is simply an additional dimension.

secoes.titulo: Skin: Pale / Tanned — and 'Dark' as Its Own Category
secoes.conteudo:
Describing skin in English is clear once you have three words: **pale**, **tanned**, and **dark**. Each means something specific.

The most interesting pair is **pale** and **tanned** — because they describe the same type of person in two different conditions. **Pale** skin is light-colored skin that does not get much sun. A person who works indoors all year, or who burns rather than tans, will have **pale** skin. **Tanned** skin is **pale** skin that has become darker through sun exposure — a beach holiday, a summer spent outdoors. **Tanned** is not someone's natural color; it is a temporary change. The pair **pale / tanned** describes the same skin across different seasons.

Then there is **dark** skin — and this is a separate category entirely. **Dark** describes someone's natural skin color, not a change from the sun. 'She has dark skin' is a neutral color description, exactly like 'she has **dark** hair.' It covers a wide range of naturally deeper skin tones and is always appropriate and respectful.

One more word, mostly British English: **spotty**. **Spotty** skin has spots or pimples. It is casual and everyday. 'He had a **spotty** complexion as a teenager' is perfectly natural in British conversation.

Native speakers almost never say just 'she is tall' and leave it there. They add a small word before the adjective to show how strong the description is. These small words are called **modifiers**, and they are everywhere in real English.

The **modifiers** you need: **really**, **very**, **so**, **quite**, **fairly**, **pretty**, and **rather**.

**Really**, **very**, and **so** make an adjective stronger. 'She is really tall.' 'He is very muscular.' 'Your hair is so curly!' These feel natural and common in everyday conversation. **So** adds a layer of emotion — it signals slight surprise or admiration. 'She is so slim!' carries more feeling than 'She is very slim.'

The more interesting group: **quite**, **fairly**, **pretty**, and **rather**. These soften an adjective — they mean 'a noticeable amount, but measured.' Each has its own personality. **Quite** is the most neutral: 'She is quite tall' means tall, calmly observed. **Fairly** is slightly more cautious: 'She is fairly slim' means slim but not dramatically so. **Pretty** — and this is important — when used as a **modifier**, has nothing to do with 'beautiful.' It simply means 'quite' or 'rather a lot,' and it is very common in American English: 'She is pretty short' means noticeably short. **Rather** sounds a bit more British and implies mild surprise: 'He was rather thin' feels like 'hm, thinner than I expected.'

Real examples, all completely natural: 'She was quite slim.' 'He has pretty curly hair.' 'I'm fairly tanned.' 'She looked rather pale.' This is the kind of English that makes people say: your English is really good.

A few things about appearance vocabulary behave differently from what you might expect.

**Slim** and **thin** again — because this distinction matters enough to repeat. Both translate to 'magro' in Portuguese. But in English, **slim** is always positive and complimentary. **Thin** is more neutral, sometimes negative — it can suggest someone looks underweight or fragile. If you want to say someone looks good, use **slim**. If you are simply making a factual observation, **thin** is fine. Choosing the right one shows a real understanding of English nuance.

**Fair**. This word has multiple lives in English. In appearance: **fair hair** = light-colored hair, **fair skin** = light skin. But **fair** also means just or equal: 'It's not fair!' It can mean acceptable but not excellent: 'The film was fair, nothing special.' And in weather: 'a fair day' means clear and pleasant. The word is the same in every context — look at the situation and the meaning is always clear.

**Pretty**. As a **modifier**, **pretty** has nothing to do with beauty — 'she is pretty short' means noticeably short. But as a straight adjective — 'she is pretty' — it means attractive. The same word does both jobs, and only context tells you which one is active. In 'he has pretty curly hair,' you need to read **pretty** as 'quite' — not as a comment on how beautiful the curls are. After a while this distinction becomes automatic, but it surprises people at first.

the natural hair color that comes with age — also spelled 'gray' in American English

lines that appear on the face with age — also called 'laughter lines' around the eyes
above average in height ↔ short

not heavy — more neutral than slim, sometimes implies concern about weight

very light skin that does not get much sun ↔ tanned

(British English) skin with spots or pimples — casual everyday word
